description: Medieval Serbian kingdom (1217–1346) under the Nemanjić dynasty that converted Serbia to Orthodox Christianity, allied with Byzantium through marriages, and built the great monastery complex at Studenica; Milutin's aggressive southern expansion and brilliant Byzantine-style propaganda frescoes established Serbia as the dominant Balkan power before Dušan's imperial proclamation.

temporal.notes: Stefan Nemanja's foundation; raised to empire under Dušan

lifecycle_phases.description: Stefan Nemanja unifies the Serbian principalities (1167) and builds the Nemanjić dynasty. He abdicates (1196) to become a monk, founding the Hilandar monastery on Mount Athos; his son Saint Sava establishes the autocephalous Serbian Orthodox Church (1219) and provides the kingdom with an independent religious identity. Stefan the First-Crowned (1217) receives a royal crown from Rome then from the Ecumenical Patriarch.

Stefan Milutin (1282–1321) dramatically expands Serbia by exploiting Byzantine weakness, annexing Macedonia. His grandson Stefan Dušan (1331–1355) continues the expansion, conquering Albania, Epirus, Thessaly, and parts of Thrace. In 1346, Dušan crowns himself 'Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks', the culmination of the Nemanjić dynasty's ambitions, though the empire immediately becomes the shorter-lived 'Serbian Empire.'

rise_factors.description: The autocephalous Serbian Orthodox Church (1219), Saint Sava's religious writings, and the proliferation of monasteries gave the Nemanjić dynasty a religious prestige that legitimized expansion into Byzantine territories; the dynasty's practice of founding major monasteries built a network of ideological centers across their domains

Byzantine civil wars and the Fourth Crusade's disruption gave the Nemanjić kings repeated opportunities to expand at Byzantine expense; each Byzantine internal crisis was matched by Serbian territorial gains in Macedonia, Albania, and Thrace

Stefan Nemanja's son Sava became the first Archbishop of Serbia (1219) and established the Serbian Orthodox Church as an autocephalous body; the national church gave the Nemanjić dynasty legitimacy combining spiritual and secular authority and preserved Serbian identity against Byzantine and Hungarian pressure

The Novo Brdo and Srebrenica silver mines (developed with Saxon mining expertise from the 13th century) made Serbia the richest silver producer in the Balkans; mine revenues funded Stefan Dušan's empire-building and the spectacular monastery construction at Dečani, Studenica, and Gračanica

Stefan Dušan (r. 1331–1355) conquered Macedonia, Epirus, Thessaly, and much of Albania; he crowned himself "Emperor of the Serbs and Romans" in 1346 and issued the Dušan's Code, the most comprehensive Balkan legal compilation, creating Serbia's greatest territorial extent

Stefan Nemanja founded the Serbian Orthodox Church and his son Saint Sava secured its autocephalous status in 1219, creating an ecclesiastical institution that legitimized Nemanjić rule and preserved Serbian cultural identity through foreign conquests.

decline_factors.description: Dušan's rapid elevation to emperor and the empire's enormous territorial expansion created a state that could not survive his death; the nobility's regional autonomy, accumulated during the rapid conquests, immediately overcame central authority

Ottoman forces reached the Balkans in 1354; the Battle of Maritsa (1371) and Kosovo Polje (1389) broke Serbian military power; though the medieval Serbian state survived as an Ottoman vassal into the 15th century, the defeat at Kosovo ended Serbian autonomy

After Dušan's death (1355) the empire fragmented among regional lords (župan); no successor could reimpose central authority, and the Nemanjić state collapsed into competing principalities that the Ottomans defeated individually

Stefan Dušan's sudden death in 1355 left an empire without institutional foundations; within years the great nobles (župans) carved out autonomous principalities, leaving Serbia politically fragmented at the worst possible time before Ottoman expansion.

sources.author: Fine, John V.A., Jr.
sources.title: The Late Medieval Balkans: A Critical Survey from the Late Twelfth Century to the Ottoman Conquest
